content.text: {"primary_meaning":"Sin most commonly signifies human rebellion against, disobedience to, and estrangement from God—an evil condition expressed in wrongful acts and resulting in corruption and death. Strictly speaking, biblical and Christian teaching usually treats sin as a theological and moral reality rather than as a symbol with one fixed symbolic referent.","primary_basis":["Genesis 3:1–24 — humanity’s disobedience produces alienation, curse, and death.","Isaiah 59:2 — iniquities separate people from God.","Romans 3:23 — all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory.","Romans 5:12–21 — sin enters the world and reigns through death.","Romans 6:16–23 — sin is portrayed as an enslaving master whose outcome is death.","1 John 3:4 — sin is identified with lawlessness.","James 1:14–15 — desire gives birth to sin, and sin brings forth death."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Sin as transgression or violation of divine law: concrete culpable acts contrary to God’s commands.","basis":["Psalm 51:1–4","Romans 4:15","1 John 3:4","James 2:9–11"],"prominence":"dominant"},{"meaning":"Sin as ‘missing the mark’ or falling short of God’s intended standard. This is a widespread explanatory gloss based especially on Greek hamartia, though many scholars regard it as incomplete if treated as the whole biblical definition.","basis":["Romans 3:23","Philippians 3:14, by analogy with goal or mark imagery"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sin as an enslaving, quasi-personified power that rules humanity rather than merely a collection of individual misdeeds.","basis":["Genesis 4:7","John 8:34","Romans 5:12–21","Romans 6:6–23","Romans 7:8–23"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sin as an inherited condition or original sin: humanity shares a fallen state traced to Adam, with traditions differing over inherited guilt, corruption, and mortality.","basis":["Genesis 3:1–24","Psalm 51:5","Romans 5:12–19","1 Corinthians 15:21–22"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sin primarily as spiritual sickness, corruption, or bondage requiring healing and restoration. This is especially prominent in Eastern Christian interpretation, though it also appears elsewhere.","basis":["Psalm 38:3–8","Isaiah 1:5–6","Mark 2:17","Romans 7:21–24"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Sin fundamentally as unbelief, idolatry, or misplaced allegiance, from which particular immoral acts proceed.","basis":["Exodus 20:3–5","Jeremiah 2:13","John 16:8–9","Romans 1:21–25","Romans 14:23"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad consensus that sin involves opposition to God and brings alienation, bondage, corruption, and death. There is no single settled symbolic interpretation because Scripture uses several overlapping legal, relational, cultic, medical, and dominion metaphors, and Christian traditions weight them differently."}
